task1.title: The formation of rain-shadow deserts
task1.prompt: The diagram below shows how one type of desert, known as a rain-shadow desert, is formed.

chartDesc.title: The formation of rain-shadow deserts

stages.label: Winds approach coast
stages.detail: Winds blow over the sea towards the coast.

stages.label: Winds pushed upwards
stages.detail: Winds are forced upwards as they encounter the slope of the mountains.

stages.label: Moist air rises and cools
stages.detail: Moist air ascends along the windward side of the mountain and cools.

stages.label: Clouds form
stages.detail: Clouds form in the sky on the windward side of the mountain.

stages.label: Rain falls
stages.detail: Rain falls from clouds onto the windward side.

stages.label: Dry air continues over mountain
stages.detail: Dry air moves across the mountain peak and down the leeward side.

stages.label: Dry winds reach inland areas
stages.detail: Dry winds descend and travel into inland areas, forming a rain-shadow desert.

chartDesc.overview: The diagram illustrates a 7-stage linear process showing how moist winds from the sea lose precipitation on the windward side of a mountain range, resulting in dry winds that form a rain-shadow desert in inland areas over thousands of kilometres.
keyFeatures: Linear process with 7 clearly numbered stages.
Shows two distinct sides of the mountain range: Windward side (where moist air rises, clouds form, and rain falls) and Leeward side (where dry air travels over to the inland region).
Labels geographical elements: Sea, Coast, Windward side, Mountains, Leeward side, Inland, and Rain-shadow desert.
Includes a scale bar at the bottom indicating distance across 'Thousands of kilometres'.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
